title: Strong Passwords
about: How passwords get guessed, and how to make yours hard to crack.

cards.prompt: A short password falls in seconds. **Drag** until cracking it would take 100+ years.
cards.explanation: Each extra letter multiplies a computer's work by **26**, so **length** is what makes a password strong.
cards.hint: Drag the slider right and watch the time shoot up.
cards.nudge: Keep going: every extra letter multiplies the time by 26.

cards.sentence: Guessers try **common passwords** like `password123`, **names and years**, and **song lines** first.

cards.prompt: Guessed early, or hard to guess?

items.label: Your pet's name and birth year
A line from a famous song

cards.explanation: Common passwords, names, years and song lines are **tried first**. Random words must be found by trying every combination.
cards.hint: Would a guesser try it early: a common password, a name, a year or a famous line?
cards.nudge: Look again: is it on a guesser's early list, or long and random?

cards.sentence: A **passphrase** is four or more **random** words, like `otter planet brick soup`: never a song line.

cards.prompt: Twist: only **10 characters** allowed. Add kinds of characters to reach **100 years**.
cards.explanation: More kinds of characters means more to try, so even a **short random** password can be strong. Long passphrases are just easier to remember.
cards.hint: Each switch adds more characters a guesser has to try.
cards.nudge: Keep adding kinds of characters until the time passes 100 years.

cards.prompt: A game site was hacked, and passwords were stolen: a [[data breach]].

steps.text: You used that password for your **email** too. What first?

choices.text: Change your email password to a new one
choices.consequence: Good. Your email is the most important account: it can reset all the others.
The same password opens your email too. Attackers try stolen passwords on other sites.
The stolen password still opens your email. That's the one to change first.

steps.text: Your email is safe. And the game?

choices.text: Give it its own new password
choices.consequence: Now each account has its own password, so one leak can't open the other.

choices.text: Use the new email password too
choices.consequence: Then the next breach could open your email again. Every account needs its own password.

cards.explanation: Change a stolen password everywhere you used it, starting with your **email**, which can reset the rest. Every account needs its **own** password.
cards.hint: Which account could be used to reset all your others?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **Length** wins: a **passphrase** is four or more **random** words.
- Give every account its **own** password.
- **Try this:** change one password you reuse into a four-word passphrase.
